read.sections.0.heading.source: Resources help people meet needs and wants
read.sections.0.heading.back: Resources help people get their needs and wants

read.sections.0.text.source: Every day, people make choices, from what to do after class to how a household uses its food, money or phone data. To make these choices, people use resources. A resource is anything useful that people have, such as time, money, food, water, tools or skills. People use resources to meet their needs and wants. A need is something you must have to live safely and stay healthy, such as food, clean water and a safe place to sleep. A want is something you would like to have but can live without. For example, Noor's aunt needs to buy rice and soap, but a new football is a want.
read.sections.0.text.back: Every day, people have to choose, from what to do after school to how a family will use food, money or phone internet. To choose, people use resources. A resource is anything useful that people have, such as time, money, food, water, tools or skills. People use resources to get their needs and wants. A need is something you must have to live safely and healthily, such as food, clean water and a safe place to sleep. A want is something you would like to have, but can live without. For example, Noor's aunt needs to buy rice and soap, but a new football is a want.

read.sections.0.simpler.source: People make choices every day. To choose, they use resources. A resource is something useful that you have. Time, money, food and skills are resources. A need is something you must have to live and stay well. A want is something you would like. You can live without it. Noor's aunt needs rice and soap. A new football is a want.
read.sections.0.simpler.back: People have to choose every day. When they choose, they use resources. A resource is a useful thing you have. Time, money, food and skills are resources. A need is something you must have to live and be well. A want is something you would like to have, but can live without. Noor's aunt has to buy rice and soap. A new football is a want.
read.sections.0.simpler.note: The simpler text is split into short clauses with spaces so that it counts as shorter sentences than the standard text, whose lists (เช่น เวลา เงิน ...) count as many one-word 'sentences' for the checker. Check the splits read naturally.

read.sections.1.text.source: Usually, people do not have enough resources for everything they need and want. This problem is called scarcity. Scarcity does not mean there is nothing; it means there is not enough for every possible use. Noor's household shares one phone with a small amount of mobile data each week. Noor needs data for her online English class, and her cousins want to watch music videos. There is not enough data for both, so the household must decide. Communities face scarcity too. Hillside Learning Centre has one free room on Tuesday afternoons, so it must choose between a homework club and an art class.
read.sections.1.text.back: Usually, people don't have enough resources for everything they need and want. This problem is called scarcity. Scarcity doesn't mean having nothing at all; it means not having enough for every possible use. Noor's family shares one phone and has little mobile internet each week. Noor needs internet for her online English class, while her cousins want to watch music videos. There isn't enough internet for both, so the family has to decide. Communities face scarcity too. Hillside Learning Centre has one free room on Tuesday afternoon, so it must choose between a homework club and an art class.

read.sections.1.simpler.source: Often there is not enough for all our needs and wants. This is called scarcity. It does not mean there is nothing. It means there is not enough for every use. Noor's home has one phone with a little data. Noor needs data for her class. Her cousins want music videos. There is not enough for both. So they must choose. A learning centre has one free room. It can hold a homework club or an art class, not both.
read.sections.1.simpler.back: Often, we don't have enough for everything we need and want. This is called scarcity. It doesn't mean having nothing at all. It means not having enough for every use. Noor's home has one phone. The phone has a little internet. She needs internet to study. Her cousins want to watch music videos. The internet isn't enough for both. So they have to choose. A learning centre has one free room. It can hold a homework club, or an art class, but not both.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Every choice has an opportunity cost
read.sections.2.heading.back: Every choice has an opportunity cost

read.sections.2.text.source: Whenever you choose one thing, you give up something else. The next-best option you give up is called the opportunity cost. On Saturday afternoon, Noor can play football with friends or practise English with a study partner. She chooses English, so her opportunity cost is the football game. Opportunity cost is not only about money; it can also be time, energy, space or another chance. Thinking about opportunity cost does not tell you which choice is correct. Instead, it helps you understand what you are giving up. Before deciding, ask: What do we need? What do we want? What will we give up?
read.sections.2.text.back: Every time you choose one thing, you have to give up another. The next-best option you give up is called opportunity cost. On Saturday afternoon, Noor could play football with friends or practise English with a friend she studies with. She chooses English, so her opportunity cost is playing football. Opportunity cost isn't only about money; it may be time, energy, space or other chances. Thinking about opportunity cost doesn't tell you which choice is right, but it helps you understand what you are giving up. Before deciding, try asking: What do we need? What do we want? What will we have to give up?
read.sections.2.text.note: 'next-best option' is ตัวเลือกที่ดีรองลงมา; the simpler text, like the English, says 'the best thing you did not pick' (สิ่งที่ดีที่สุดที่คุณไม่ได้เลือก). ค่าเสียโอกาส is the Thai economics term (KEY_TERMS). The three closing questions keep their question marks.

read.sections.2.simpler.source: When you choose one thing, you give up another. The best thing you did not pick is the opportunity cost. On Saturday, Noor can play football. Or she can practise English with a friend. She picks English. So the football game is her opportunity cost. Opportunity cost is not only about money. It can be time or space too. It does not tell you the right choice. It shows what you give up.
read.sections.2.simpler.back: When you choose one thing, you lose another. The best thing you did not choose is the opportunity cost. On Saturday, Noor can play football, or practise English with a friend. She chooses English. So playing football is her opportunity cost. Opportunity cost isn't only about money. It may be time or space. It doesn't tell you which choice is right. It tells you what you lost.

write.example.source: The choice is between Noor's online English class and music videos for her cousins. The limited resource is the mobile data on the one phone they share. watch.summary.source: This short video explains opportunity cost. When you pick one thing, you cannot have another. The next-best thing you give up is your opportunity cost. In the video, a young man called Mario needs a new phone. He also wants a new games console. His money is not enough for both, so he has to choose. He could buy a cheaper phone and get both things. But then his phone has fewer features. That is his opportunity cost. The video also shows that time can be a cost, not only money. It says the real cost of a choice is more than its price. Thinking about opportunity cost helps you compare needs and wants before you decide.
watch.summary.back: This short video explains opportunity cost. When you choose one thing, you don't get another. The next-best thing you give up is your opportunity cost. In the video, a young man called Mario needs a new phone. He also wants a new game console. He doesn't have enough money for both, so he has to choose. He could buy a cheaper phone and get both, but the phone would have fewer functions. That is his opportunity cost. The video also shows that time can be a cost too, not just money. The video says the real cost of a choice is more than its price. Thinking about opportunity cost helps you compare needs and wants before you decide.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: The video comes from ABC Australia's money series for teenagers (also shown as My Five Cents). Its example is a young man, Mario, who needs a new phone and wants a games console, and one option it gives is working an extra shift at his job. Preview it: if this does not fit your learners, use the written summary, which leaves out the job, and the lesson's own examples.
